---
title: "Style Guide"
---

Every team has Python conventions a linter can't express, like banning `print()` in committed code, bare `except:`, and `import *`. captain-hook ships *no* rules of its own. You author them as `StyleRule` subclasses and hand them to `styleguide()`, which parses each edited file, runs every rule, and reports only the violations your edit actually introduced.

<!-- gd-embed: styleguide.py -->

The `styleguide()` call registers one PostToolUse hook that fires after every Python edit. A rule is a subclass whose docstring is the message, where `{violations}` is substituted at fire time and the docstring doubles as the rule's API-reference text. The class name `NoPrint` becomes the identity `no-print`. Each rule is data. Set `match` to a composable matcher built from the `matchers` module, imported `as M` with an optional `label`, and the base class does the walking. `NoPrint` is `M.calls("print")`, and `NoBareExcept` refines a node type with a one-off predicate via `.where(...)`. The runner renders `label (line N)` and drops any violation whose line you didn't touch, so editing one function never lights up a pre-existing `print()` elsewhere in the file. `NoNewWildcardImport` subclasses `StyleDiffRule` to flag nodes matching `match` in the new tree that weren't in the old one, reporting only what the edit *added*. Reach for an explicit `check()` method when a rule's logic can't be expressed as a matcher. One `styleguide(...)` call registers one hook; pass `block=True` or scope it with `only_if=` to register a second, differently scoped hook. See also [the style guide](../guide/styleguide.qmd) and [the conditions guide](../guide/conditions.qmd) for scoping hooks.
